title: Chapter 13 — Wheelbarrow
paragraphs: Next morning, Monday, after disposing of the embalmed head to a barber, for use as a wig block, I settled my own and my comrade's bill — using, however, my comrade's money. The grinning landlord, as well as the boarders, seemed amazingly tickled by the sudden friendship that had sprung up between me and Queequeg — especially as Peter Coffin's cock-and-bull stories about him had earlier alarmed me so much about the very person I now kept company with.

We borrowed a wheelbarrow, and loading our things into it, including my own poor carpetbag and Queequeg's canvas sack and hammock, off we went down to "the Moss," the little Nantucket packet schooner moored at the wharf. As we went along, people stared — not so much at Queequeg, for they were used to seeing cannibals like him in their streets, but at seeing him and me on such confidential terms. But we paid them no attention, going along wheeling the barrow by turns, with Queequeg now and then stopping to adjust the sheath on his harpoon barbs. I asked him why he carried such a troublesome thing with him ashore, and whether all whaling ships did not supply their own harpoons. To this, in substance, he replied that though what I suggested was true enough, he had a particular affection for his own harpoon, because it was made of reliable stuff, well tried in many a mortal combat, and deeply intimate with the hearts of whales. In short, like many inland reapers and mowers who go into the farmers' meadows armed with their own scythes — though in no way obliged to supply them — just so Queequeg, for his own private reasons, preferred his own harpoon.

Shifting the barrow from my hand to his, he told me a funny story about the first wheelbarrow he had ever seen. It was in Sag Harbor. The owners of his ship, it seems, had lent him one to carry his heavy chest to his boarding house. So as not to seem ignorant about the thing — though in truth he was entirely ignorant of exactly how to manage a barrow — Queequeg puts his chest on it, lashes it fast, and then shoulders the barrow and marches up the wharf. "Why, Queequeg," I said, "you might have known better than that, one would think. Didn't the people laugh?"

At this, he told me another story. The people of his island of Rokovoko, it seems, at their wedding feasts press the fragrant water of young coconuts into a large stained calabash like a punchbowl; and this punchbowl always forms the great central ornament on the braided mat where the feast is held. Now a certain grand merchant ship once touched at Rokovoko, and its commander — by all accounts a very stately, punctilious gentleman, at least for a sea captain — this commander was invited to the wedding feast of Queequeg's sister, a pretty young princess just turned ten. Well, when all the wedding guests were assembled at the bride's bamboo cottage, this Captain marches in, and being given the place of honor, sets himself opposite the punchbowl, between the High Priest and his majesty the King, Queequeg's father. Grace being said — for those people have their grace as well as we do, though Queequeg told me that unlike us, who at such times look down at our plates, they, on the contrary, copying the ducks, glance upward to the great Giver of all feasts — grace, I say, being said, the High Priest opens the banquet with the immemorial ceremony of the island; that is, dipping his consecrated and consecrating fingers into the bowl before the blessed drink goes around. Seeing himself placed next to the Priest, and noting the ceremony, and thinking that he — being Captain of a ship — plainly took precedence over a mere island King, especially in the King's own house, the Captain coolly proceeds to wash his hands in the punchbowl, taking it, I suppose, for a huge finger bowl. "Now," said Queequeg, "what you tink now? Didn't our people laugh?"

Finally, with our fare paid and our luggage safe, we stood on board the schooner. She hoisted sail and slid down the Acushnet River. On one side New Bedford climbed in terraces of streets, the ice-coated trees all sparkling in the clear, cold air. Enormous hills and mountains of casks upon casks were stacked on her wharves, and side by side the world-roaming whale ships lay silent and at last safely moored; while from others came the sounds of carpenters and coopers, mixed with the noise of fires and forges melting pitch — all signs that new voyages were getting under way; that the end of one long and deeply dangerous voyage only begins a second, and the end of the second only begins a third, and so on, forever and ever. Such is the endlessness — yes, the unbearableness — of all earthly effort.

Once we reached the more open water, the bracing breeze grew fresh; the little Moss tossed the quick foam from her bows, as a young colt tosses his snortings. How I sniffed that Tartar air! How I spurned that turnpike earth — that common highway dented all over with the marks of slavish heels and hoofs — and turned to admire the magnanimity of the sea, which will permit no records.

Queequeg seemed to drink and reel with me at the same foam-fountain. His dusky nostrils swelled apart; he showed his filed and pointed teeth. On, on we flew; and once we had gained the offing, the Moss paid homage to the blast, ducking and diving her bows like a slave before the Sultan. Leaning sideways, we darted sideways; every rope-yarn tingling like a wire; the two tall masts buckling like Indian canes in land tornadoes. We were so full of this reeling scene, as we stood by the plunging bowsprit, that for some time we did not notice the jeering glances of the passengers, a lubberly crowd, who marveled that two fellow beings should be so companionable — as though a white man were anything more dignified than a whitewashed negro. But there were some boobies and bumpkins there who, by their intense greenness, must have come from the very heart and center of all green growing things. Queequeg caught one of these young saplings mimicking him behind his back. I thought the bumpkin's hour of doom had come. Dropping his harpoon, the brawny savage caught him in his arms, and with an almost miraculous dexterity and strength sent him bodily high into the air; then, with a slight tap on his rear in mid-somersault, the fellow landed on his feet with bursting lungs, while Queequeg, turning his back on him, lit his tomahawk pipe and passed it to me for a puff.
"Capting! Capting!" yelled the bumpkin, running toward that officer. "Capting, Capting, here's the devil."
"Hey, you there, sir," cried the Captain, a gaunt rib of the sea, stalking up to Queequeg, "what in thunder do you mean by that? Don't you know you might have killed that fellow?"
"What him say?" said Queequeg, mildly turning to me.
"He say," I said, "that you came near kill-e that man there," pointing to the still-shivering greenhorn.
"Kill-e," cried Queequeg, twisting his tattooed face into an unearthly look of disdain, "ah! him very small-e fish-e; Queequeg no kill-e so small-e fish-e; Queequeg kill-e big whale!"
"Look here," roared the Captain, "I'll kill-e you, you cannibal, if you try any more of your tricks aboard here; so mind your eye."

But just then, as it happened, it was high time for the Captain to look out for himself. The enormous strain on the mainsail had snapped the weather-sheet, and the huge boom was now swinging wildly from side to side, sweeping clean across the whole after part of the deck. The poor fellow Queequeg had treated so roughly was knocked overboard; the whole crew panicked; and trying to grab the boom to stop it looked like madness. It flew from right to left and back again in hardly more than a single tick of a watch, and every instant it seemed about to shatter into splinters. Nobody did anything, and nothing seemed possible to do; the people on deck ran toward the bows and stood staring at the boom as if it were the lower jaw of an enraged whale. In the middle of this alarm, Queequeg dropped neatly to his knees, crawled under the path of the boom, grabbed a rope, made one end fast to the bulwarks, then flung the other end like a lasso and caught it around the boom as it swept over his head; at the next jerk the spar was trapped, and everything was safe. The schooner was turned into the wind, and while the crew were clearing away the stern boat, Queequeg, stripped to the waist, shot off the side in a long, living arc of a leap. For three minutes or more he could be seen swimming like a dog, flinging his long arms straight out ahead of him, his powerful shoulders showing now and then through the freezing foam. I looked at this grand and glorious fellow, but saw no one to save. The greenhorn had gone under. Launching himself straight up out of the water, Queequeg glanced around him for an instant, and appearing to grasp exactly how things stood, dove down and vanished. A few minutes later he came up again, one arm still stroking, the other dragging a lifeless body. The boat soon picked them both up. The poor bumpkin was brought back to life. The whole crew declared Queequeg a noble trump; the captain begged his pardon. From that hour I stuck to Queequeg like a barnacle — yes, until poor Queequeg took his last long dive.

Was there ever such unself-consciousness? He did not seem to think that he in any way deserved a medal from the Humane and Magnanimous Societies. He only asked for water — fresh water — something to wipe the brine off; that done, he put on dry clothes, lit his pipe, and leaning against the bulwarks and mildly eyeing those around him, seemed to be saying to himself: "It's a mutual, joint-stock world, in all meridians. We cannibals must help these Christians."
